items.title: Wheel-rail dynamic interaction in high-speed railway systems: a comprehensive review of stability, safety and wear evolution
items.abstract: Purpose The wheel–rail (WR) dynamic interaction is fundamental to ensuring the stability, safety, and long-term performance of high-speed railway (HSR) systems. When operating speeds exceed 300 km/h, the vehicle-track system experiences pronounced nonlinear contact phenomena, transient dynamic effects, and continuous variations in WR interface conditions, directly affecting hunting stability, derailment risk, wear progression, and maintenance requirements. Design/methodology/approach The theoretical foundations, numerical modelling approaches, and experimental techniques related to WR dynamic interaction under high-speed conditions are systematically presented. Major WR contact theories are examined, including the Hertzian normal contact model and tangential contact formulations based on Kalker's theory together with modern nonlinear approaches. These methods are compared in terms of accuracy, capability to represent contact behaviour, and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the integration of vehicle-track dynamic models and long-term wear evolution models is analysed in order to clarify the relationship between geometric degradation and the dynamic stability of the system. Findings Key safety assessment criteria are discussed in the context of high-speed operation. The comparative analysis highlights the respective strengths and limitations of existing contact modelling approaches and emphasises the importance of coupling dynamic simulation with wear evolution for accurately evaluating vehicle stability and safety. Originality/value Emerging research trends, including digital twins, artificial intelligence, and multiphysics modelling, are reviewed to identify potential directions for future investigations. The review provides a comprehensive overview of current WR dynamic interaction research and offers a valuable reference for advancing the stability, safety, and maintenance strategies of future HSR systems.

An inadvertent safeguard refers to a counterintuitive scenario in which an AI error at the diagnosis/classification stage nevertheless produces a correct downstream decision recommendation. In this paper, we analyze the structural relationship between the AI's classification space and its recommendation outputs. We formalize the conditions under which inadvertent safeguards arise and compare the performance implications of Stage 3 action-selection support versus Stage 2 information-analysis support.BackgroundRecent research in human-automation and human-AI interaction has allowed for the structural possibility of inadvertent safeguards. However, this phenomenon has not been explicitly theorized or systematically examined.MethodWe first characterized the structural conditions under which inadvertent safeguards arise. We then conducted an experiment in which 90 participants completed a mental rotation task with a simulated AI decision aid that provided either Stage 2 information-analysis support or Stage 3 action-selection support.ResultsWhen inadvertent safeguards occur, Stage 3 action-selection support produced better performance, faster responses, and more positive trust adjustment than Stage 2 information-analysis support. Overall, Stage 3 action-selection support also produced higher perceived reliability, post-condition trust, and usability ratings.ConclusionThe impact of AI errors depends not only on classification accuracy but also on the mapping structure between classifications and actions. Many-to-one mappings, together with misclassifications between recommendation-equivalent states, can preserve correct downstream recommendations despite classification errors.ApplicationDesigners should distinguish classification accuracy from recommendation accuracy when evaluating Stage 3 action-selection support, especially in domains where multiple states can map to the same action.

items.title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
items.abstract: Predictive AI models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict, but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge.

items.title: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams
items.abstract: Artificial systems increasingly participate in organizational work as recurrent contributors to interdependent activity, yet research remains fragmented across system capabilities, individual responses, episodic interactions, and constructs derived from human-only teams. This article develops Organismic Human-Artificial Intelligence (OHAI) as a bounded integrative theoretical framework for studying collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams. Its focal unit is a bounded collective of distinguishable human and artificial contributors whose interdependent activity extends across successive cycles and whose prior collective activity can affect later artificial participation. The framework distinguishes system configuration, collective functioning, and collective intelligence (CI) as analytical objects, with CI as its primary theoretical target. CI denotes a general group-level capacity manifested across diverse tasks within a specified and empirically qualified task universe. Task performances may provide indicators for estimating CI or serve as external criteria, while the framework separately examines broader employee, team, and organizational consequences, including changes in human working relationships and employee wellbeing. Its central inferential rule is that a property implemented in an artificial component does not by itself establish a corresponding team-level phenomenon. Collective functioning must instead be demonstrated in the enacted organization and use of distributed contributions. Partner modeling, transactive-memory-system-related coordination, and shared-mental-model-related representational alignment provide selective lenses on such functioning. Persistence makes collective history consequential, bringing recursive updating, overlapping timescales, reconfiguration, and collective-intelligence trajectories into view without presuming adaptation or improvement. Human-only teams serve as secondary epistemic references for bounded tests of observable-pattern and functional correspondence, while relational-pattern correspondence remains a limited future methodological possibility. The empirical program distinguishes four nonmandatory stages of research maturity: configuration and measurement qualification, local relations, longitudinal team-level phenomena, and integrated multilevel studies. The framework thereby provides a disciplined basis for cumulative research on how heterogeneous contributions become collectively consequential and change over time.

items.title: When hybrid (ChatGPT and teacher) feedback does not outperform teacher-only feedback: evidence from A2 EFL writing in Ecuador
items.abstract: This study investigated whether hybrid (ChatGPT-generated and teacher-provided) feedback could yield greater gains in grammatical accuracy than teacher-only feedback among on-site A2-level English as a foreign language (EFL) students at a technical higher education institute in Quito, Ecuador. A six-week quasi-experimental study involved 41 students from two intact classes: teacher-only ( n = 18) and hybrid feedback ( n = 23). Both groups completed six handwritten writing tasks. Initial feedback was provided in English by the teacher or ChatGPT. Students in both groups reviewed this feedback using the textbook, class notes, and teacher clarification in English and Spanish as needed before rewriting their sentences. All students completed the same 18-item Grammar Accuracy Writing Test before and after the intervention. The test assessed verb tense usage, word order, subject-verb agreement, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions. Both groups improved from pretest to posttest. Teacher-only scores increased from M = 7.17 to M = 9.61 and hybrid scores from M = 9.17 to M = 10.78. The unadjusted gain difference (hybrid minus teacher-only) was −0.84 points [95% confidence interval (−2.68, 1.00), p = 0.364]. Analysis of covariance controlling for pretest scores also detected no statistically significant difference [adjusted mean difference = −0.40 points, 95% confidence interval (−2.25, 1.45), p = 0.664]. None of the six grammatical-category comparisons reached statistical significance after Holm correction. Interpretation is limited by the small sample, intact classes with different schedules, repeated use of the same test, and scoring by one non-blinded rater. The confidence intervals include effects favoring either condition, so the nonsignificant results should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. The study did not detect a statistically significant advantage for hybrid feedback in this A2 EFL context. Because both conditions included teacher mediation, the findings do not isolate the independent contribution of ChatGPT. Future research should examine longer interventions, larger samples, and how learners interpret and apply AI-generated feedback.

items.title: When Nobody Knows What Is Real: Associations Between AI-Generated Manipulation, Fear of AI Fraud, Privacy Protection Behavior, and Trust in AI Governance
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified concerns regarding misinformation, identity fraud, privacy, and public trust in AI governance. This study examines the associations among perceived exposure to AI-generated manipulation, fear of AI fraud, privacy protection behavior, and trust in AI governance. Informed by Protection Motivation Theory, a theoretically specified sequential model of associations among Exposure to AI Manipulation, Fear of AI Fraud, Privacy Protection Behavior, and Trust in AI Governance was evaluated. Data were collected from 2683 respondents across ten countries using Prolific. The measurement model was assessed through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, while the proposed associations were examined using covariance-based structural equation modeling and bootstrap analysis of specific indirect associations. Perceived exposure to AI manipulation was positively associated with fear of AI fraud, which was positively associated with privacy protection behavior. Privacy protection behavior was positively associated with trust in AI governance. However, exposure was not directly associated with privacy protection behavior or trust, while fear was not directly associated with trust. Significant specific indirect and sequential indirect associations were identified within the specified model and should be interpreted as model-dependent statistical associations. Interpreted through the lens of Protection Motivation Theory, the findings identify a theoretically consistent pattern of associations among perceived technological exposure, AI-related fear, privacy-protective behavior, and institutional trust. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations do not establish temporal or causal ordering among the constructs.

items.title: Work-related Musculoskeletal Pain Among Physiotherapy Interns: A Cross-sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: Physiotherapy is a physically demanding profession that places practitioners at risk of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Pain (WRMSP). During internships, physiotherapy interns frequently engage in patient handling, repetitive therapeutic procedures, prolonged standing, and awkward postures, increasing their susceptibility to musculoskeletal pain. Early identification of WRMSP and its associated factors is essential for implementing preventive strategies and promoting long-term occupational well-being. Objective: To determine the prevalence of work-related musculoskeletal pain among physiotherapy interns and identify its associated risk factors. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 99 physiotherapy interns in selected clinical settings in Bangalore using convenience sampling. Data on demographic characteristics, work-related factors, ergonomic training, pain characteristics, and a standardized body pain chart were collected. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data, while Chi-square tests, independent t-tests, and odds ratio analyses assessed associations between variables. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: WRMSP was highly prevalent among physiotherapy interns. The lower back was the most commonly affected region (71%), followed by the neck (39%), upper back (21%), shoulder (17%), and wrist (7%). A significant association was found between the absence of ergonomic training and the occurrence of WRMSP (χ² = 7.12, p = 0.008). Female interns reported significantly higher pain scores than male interns (t = 2.05, p = 0.043). Interns treating eight or more patients per day were 3.5 times more likely to experience frequent or constant pain (OR = 3.5; 95% CI: 1.4–8.9; p = 0.007). Common contributing factors included poor posture, repetitive tasks, prolonged standing, patient handling, and heavy workload. Conclusion: WRMSP is highly prevalent among physiotherapy interns, particularly affecting the lower back. High patient load, inadequate ergonomic training, poor posture, repetitive activities, and prolonged standing contribute significantly to its development. Incorporating ergonomic education, safe patient-handling techniques, and self-care strategies into physiotherapy training programs may help reduce WRMSP and promote occupational health among future physiotherapists. Major Findings: Work-related musculoskeletal pain was highly prevalent among physiotherapy interns, suggesting that musculoskeletal problems may begin early in their professional careers. The lower back (71%) and neck (39%) were the most commonly affected regions, indicating significant physical demands during clinical training. Higher patient load and lack of ergonomic training were significantly associated with WRMSP, highlighting the importance of workload management and ergonomic education in internship programs.

items.title: Writing trust in the age of generative AI: special interest magazines and embodied expertise
items.abstract: This article examines how English-language cycling magazines rhetorically negotiate generative AI. Drawing on interpretive rhetorical analysis of purposively selected, publicly accessible reader-facing materials, it argues that AI poses a distinctive challenge because the authority of special interest magazines depends on recognisable human authorship, embodied expertise and reader trust. It develops the ‘slow middle’ as a conceptual framework for understanding how these publications position themselves within careful, expert and community-oriented cultural production, distinct from automated, high-volume online content. Viewed through this framework, two recurring rhetorical patterns emerge from the textual sample: limited public disclosure concerning AI's role in editorial production; and the positioning of AI as an object of scrutiny, tool for reader utility or topic of coverage, rather than an authorial presence. These patterns demonstrate how special interest magazines preserve claims to human expertise and trustworthy narrative authority while remaining formative rhetorical environments for communal responses to technological change.

items.abstract: Аннотация. В статье рассматриваются изменения требований к кадровому потенциалу торговых предприятий в условиях цифровой трансформации. Анализируется влияние автоматизации, искусственного интеллекта, маркетплейсов и цифровых платформ на содержание трудовых функций и компетенции работников. Особое внимание уделяется формированию нового профиля цифровых компетенций, развитию механизмов up-skilling и re-skilling, а также внедрению современных форм цифрового обучения персонала. Обосновывается необходимость перехода от преимущественно внешнего найма к системному развитию кадров внутри организации. Предложен комплексный подход к управлению развитием персонала, включающий аудит цифровых компетенций, формирование матрицы навыков, непрерывное обучение и оценку его влияния на операционные показатели торгового предприятия. Abstract. This article examines changing requirements for the workforce of retail enterprises amidst digital transformation. It analyzes the impact of automation, artificial intelligence, marketplaces, and digital platforms on job functions and employee competencies. Particular attention is paid to defining a new digital competency profile, developing upskilling and reskilling mechanisms, and implementing modern forms of digital staff training. A comprehensive approach to managing staff development is proposed, encompassing a digital competency audit, the creation of a skills matrix, continuous learning, and an assessment of its impact on the retail enterprise's operational performance. items.abstract: The existential theory of the reals asks whether polynomial constraints with integer coefficients have a real solution. We give a proof placing this problem in the counting hierarchy. The first argument is intended to expose the essential steps, and a separate analysis lowers the bound to $\exists \mathbb{R}\subseteq\textsf{BPP}^{\textsf C_3\textsf P}\subseteq\textsf C_4\textsf P$, the fourth level of the hierarchy. For each fixed $w$, sentences with $w$ alternating real quantifier blocks lie in $\textsf C_{9w+17}\textsf P$. We then treat exact semidefinite feasibility, PosSLP, square-root sum, geometric real counting, Euler characteristic, and complex feasibility in separate applications. The corresponding bounds include $\textsf{BPP}^{\textsf C_2\textsf P}$ for general SDP, $\textsf{BPP}^{\textsf{PP}}\cap\textsf{P}^{\textsf{NP}^{\textsf{PP}}}$ for PosSLP and square-root sum, and $\textsf{FP}^{\textsf C_4\textsf P}$ for total geometric real counting. Note: These proofs were discovered by ChatGPT after a series of conversations ending on September 29th 2026. A group of researchers has been working to digest the proof, and while the most essential arguments appear correct, we are endeavoring to give this result the treatment it deserves and a proper exposition and development to benefit of the community. However, on October 6th, OpenAI released a very similar result, with a slightly weaker bound. While we work to improve our exposition of this proof, the current version has been uploaded as a service to the community to compare the different proof techniques. While the listed author takes responsibility that the proofs appear to be correct, he has not played a nontrivial role in developing them, and believes the human value will be in good exposition and canonicalization of the results.

items.title: A Chat Assistant for Software Exploration in a 3D Software Visualization
items.abstract: We present a chat assistant for interactive software exploration, embedded in the 3D software visualization tool ExplorViz. The assistant builds upon current Large Language Models (LLMs) and enables users to ask questions about the currently visualized software system and trigger actions that change the visualization through natural language. We integrate the chat assistant in our ExplorViz frontend using the CopilotKit libraries such that probabilistic LLMs are combined with deterministic and tool-based actions similar to implementations using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The chat assistant is also enabled to restructure the software system by adding, removing, or modifying parts of the software system in the visualization. An empirical experiment with eleven participants evaluated both perceived comprehension support and the tool calls that were triggered by the chat assistant. Participants rated the assistant's generated summaries and explanations as largely correct. They also reported high usability for actions like highlighting entities in the visualization and the creation of new color themes. In contrast, open-ended chat-assisted software restructuring in the visualization showed mixed results. This suggests a need for stronger guardrails for the employed LLM and better incorporation of user feedback. Overall, the assistant was perceived as usable and promising for reducing interaction overhead during exploratory program comprehension tasks. We provide a video presenting the chat assistant's use and a reproduction package of the software system that was used in our evaluation.

items.title: A Co-word Analysis of ISC-Indexed Research in Occupational Health and Safety
items.abstract: Introduction: The conceptual structure of vocabulary refers to a network of semantic associations between words, illustrating how concepts and terms are interconnected within a text or dataset. A conceptual structure is a framework that reveals how words construct meaning together and determines which concepts are most significant. Examining the conceptual structure of occupational health and safety (OHS) is of considerable importance. Consequently, this study aims to understand trends in OHS within the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC) database from 1998 to 2023 and to identify key sub- domains and dimensions of the OHS concept. Material and Methods: This research was conducted using bibliometric techniques and co-word analysis. 1,148 documents were retrieved from the ISC database to identify the conceptual structure and dominant thematic clusters related to occupational health and Safety. Cluster analysis and strategic diagrams were employed to map the conceptual structure of the research and to identify sub-domains and their relationships within this field. Results: The findings revealed twelve distinct clusters: (1) Organizational ethics and spirituality, (2) Work environment and safety, (3) Work-family conflict and quality of life, (4) Job satisfaction and employee retention, (5) Occupational stress and psychological capital, (6) Job burnout and ergonomics, (7) Job satisfaction in academic environments, (8) Work-life balance, (9) Occupational health, (10) Productivity and organizational culture, (11) Workplace challenges and career futures, and (12) Women’s employment. Conclusion: The findings revealed that work-family conflict and career-related challenges constitute the mature and central core (first quadrant) of this field in Iran, indicating a paradigm shift in studies from physical safety toward psychosocial hazards. The domain of women’s employment emerged as a specialized yet isolated area (second quadrant). Classic subjects, such as the workplace and occupational safety, alongside stress and occupational health (third quadrant), remain highly fragmented and require theoretical cohesion. Furthermore, organizational ethics and spirituality (fourth quadrant) represent a high-potential area that necessitates further theoretical development. Ultimately, the primary research gap and priority for future studies lie in integrating physical safety with mental health, as well as incorporating novel digital safety technologies to address the current void within the conceptual network.

items.title: A Deafening Silence: Catastrophic Forgetting Lives in the Output Embeddings of Tokens the Data Never Speaks
items.abstract: Continual pre-training and fine-tuning in Large Language Models (LLMs) inevitably induce catastrophic forgetting, typically mitigated by replay using often-inaccessible original data. In this data-free regime, we analyze where forgetting occurs and why. Systematic parameter freezing across five settings up to 1.4B reveals that forgetting concentrates selectively in the output embeddings of tokens rarely seen in the new corpus, whereas the same sqrt(v-hat) band of the body is inert and new learning resides elsewhere. This localization is governed by the vocabulary deficiency of the corpus rather than the training mode, allowing pre-retraining risk ranking from token counts alone within a fixed base model. Mechanistically, absent tokens receive persistent one-sided softmax gradients that Adam's second-moment (sqrt(v-hat)) normalization amplifies into full-sized updates. We therefore propose an intervention: raising Adam's epsilon exclusively for the output projection during training. Across eight settings spanning 160M to 12B parameters and four model families, this removes 39.4% to 67.9% of forgetting across all seven stable configurations without degrading target learning or requiring per-model tuning. The defense combines additively or better with replay (79.8% on Qwen/Korean) and rescues released-head LoRA from a 23-fold forgetting surge. Because post-hoc editing of the drifted rows recovers under 5% of forgetting, the intervention must operate during training. Our findings indicate that a single-line optimizer adjustment may serve as the primary defense against catastrophic forgetting where the corpus starves the vocabulary.

items.title: A Framework for the Systematic Review of ML Assets in AI Registries
items.abstract: Background: Modern software systems increasingly rely on Machine Learning (ML) assets (i.e., pre-trained models, datasets, benchmarks) for building, evaluating, and integrating ML-based systems. However, current exploration, selection and reuse practices of ML assets are not supported by systematic retrieval methodologies comparable to those used in traditional evidence synthesis. Consequently, in practice, ML asset selection is often presented as a settled design decision, supported by informal justification rather than a traceable, evidence-based, and updatable selection process. Aims: This paper explores how systematic review methods can support ML asset retrieval. In doing so, we aim to make their selection transparent and reproducible, grounded in explicit evidence, and ultimately better suited to its intended use. Method: We analyze established systematic review practices from scientific literature and adapt their phases (i.e., planning, conducting, and documenting) to Artificial Intelligence (AI) registries, treating ML assets as first-class units of analysis. The resulting framework integrates registry-aware search strategies, cross-registry schema alignment, and dependency-driven ML asset exploration. Results: We conceptualize ML asset retrieval as a systematic and reproducible process rather than an ad hoc activity, and propose a framework for structured ML asset discovery. \textbf{Conclusions:} This work illustrates how systematic review principles can be extended beyond scientific literature to support evidence synthesis over evolving AI registries.

items.title: A longitudinal comparison of shared and private e-scooter crashes, near-miss rates, attributions and characteristics
items.abstract: As e-scooters have become increasingly common in urban areas, safety concerns have grown. However, most safety research does not distinguish between shared and private e-scooter use. Moreover, no studies have examined within-person changes in safety outcomes over time. This study followed Australian e-scooter riders (n = 285) across two survey waves conducted 12 months apart (follow-up and final) and comprised two analyses. First, we compared riders’ most recent near misses and crashes on shared and private e-scooters in terms of their characteristics and riders’ attributions. At follow-up, 32.7% of participants were private-only riders, 51.2% shared-only, and 16.1% mixed-use. Most near misses involved another road user (78.1% at follow-up, 70.1% at final), while a substantial share of crashes did not (55.6%, 59.1%). Private e-scooters accounted for the majority of near misses involving another road user at both waves (64.0%, 76.6%). Near misses occurring on shared e-scooters were consistently attributed to riders’ own lack of experience. Second, we modelled within-person changes in near-miss rates. A Poisson generalised linear mixed model, with a random intercept for participant and riding exposure as an offset, tested whether near-miss rate changed between waves, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Near-miss rate did not differ significantly between waves. Riders outside Queensland and Victoria had a lower rate than Queensland riders (IRR = 0.27). Riders with primary/secondary or bachelor’s degree education were associated with lower rates than those with post-school qualifications. Riders’ attribution of shared e-scooter incidents to inexperience suggests onboarding and practical training warrant further evaluation.

items.title: A novel fluid-bladder backpack interface mitigates biomechanical loading during load carriage: A musculoskeletal modeling study
items.abstract: Traditional backpacks often cause altered gait, increased joint loading, and discomfort due to poor biomechanical load transfer. This study designed and evaluated a novel backpack featuring a soft polymer fluid-filled bladder as an ergonomic interface, assessing its impact on lower extremity biomechanics across incremental loads. Ten healthy males walked under four conditions: unloaded, and with the backpack loaded at 3 kg, 6 kg, and 9 kg. Motion capture and force plate data informed a subject-specific OpenSim model. Analyses estimated peak joint angles, muscle forces, and joint reaction loads. A repeated-measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction was used to assess the effect of load. Increasing load significantly raised hip, knee, and ankle joint reaction forces along primary weight-bearing axes and major antigravity muscle forces (e.g., quadriceps). Kinematic adaptations included increased hip and knee flexion. Critically, the load transmission pattern suggested the fluid-bladder may provide a dynamic buffering effect, showing a non-uniform force increase between mid and high loads rather than a purely linear rise. While load carriage elevates biomechanical demand, the fluid-bladder interface demonstrates potential as an ergonomic solution by potentially improving force distribution. Future work directly comparing this design to a traditional backpack is required to confirm its ergonomic advantages. This design merges functional hydration with biomechanically-informed load carriage to enhance comfort.

items.title: A RAG-Based Decision Support System for Occupational Exposure Assessment of VOCs: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
items.abstract: Introduction: Assessing exposure to volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in workplaces requires timely access to accurate, standardized guidance on sampling and analysis. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a decision-support chatbot, based on the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture, to assist occupational health professionals in selecting appropriate sampling and analysis methods for VOCs in accordance with NIOSH guidelines. Material and Methods: This research was of an applied-developmental type. In this study, relevant NIOSH methods for sampling and analysis of VOCs were extracted, structured, and organized into a knowledge base. User needs were identified through semi-structured interviews with occupational health professionals. Based on this data, a generative AI-based chatbot was designed and implemented using the RAG architecture. The system performance was evaluated using expert evaluation and a chatbot usability questionnaire. Results: The developed chatbot received an overall user-friendliness score of 3.88 out of 5, indicating good user acceptance. Participants noted improved access speed for standard technical information and the high transparency of the system’s responses. Expert evaluation also confirmed the scientific validity of the retrieved content and its compliance with NIOSH standards. Conclusion: The proposed RAG-based decision-making chatbot provides an effective and innovative tool to support occupational exposure assessment to VOCs. Integrating generative AI with standard occupational health guidelines can improve the efficiency of decision-making and access to expert information in practice.

items.title: A Scale For Value Alignment In Human-AI Interaction
items.abstract: Value alignment is a central objective in AI and HCI research, yet no validated instrument measures how users perceive it. This gap hampers the comparison and accumulation of findings and limits the effectiveness of applications, where understanding users' viewpoints is critical. We construct and evaluate a 13-item psychometric scale that measures perceived value alignment across two components: value understanding and value manifestation. It is based on a large item pool drawn from prior empirical studies, filtered by experts, and finally assessed by users (N=607) across diverse AI scenarios. Confirmatory factor analysis on an independent sample (N=259) confirmed the two-factor structure and high internal consistency for both subscales. Using optimization, we also derived a 6-item short form for quick administration. The scale is a reliable measure, providing HCI researchers with a common evaluation metric across contexts.

items.title: A sustainable profession: a qualitative exploration of peer experiences and the value of lived experience among the peer support workforce
items.abstract: Peer support workers have become an integral part of harm reduction and behavioral health services, offering support to people who use drugs (PWUD) rooted in lived experience. Unlike traditional providers, peers use lived experience as a type of experiential expertise to foster trust and credibility amongst PWUD. Peer roles have become increasingly formalized through certification and credentialing. However, discrepancies between the value of lived experience and its translation into professional work settings have not been adequately explored. This paper explores the experiences of peers and peer supervisors working in Maryland harm reduction settings using Borkman’s (1976) concept of “experiential expertise” as a framework to guide analysis. Data were collected through 30 in-depth interviews with peers (n=18) and peer supervisors (n=12) across county health departments and nonprofit organizations. Using abductive thematic analysis, and an open coding format through MAXQDA, we identified three core themes. The three core themes identified: (1) lived experience and credentialing, (2) career advancement and supervision, and (3) motivation versus pay. These findings illustrated the value of lived and professional expertise in the peer workforce. Participants emphasized the unique contribution of lived experience when building connections with PWUD, while stating the importance of credentialing in gaining institutional recognition. However, career advancement pathways remained narrow with many positions that require higher education or being limited to a supervisory role. Peers also reported experiencing organizational stagnation, perceiving peer work to be a stepping stone rather than a long-term career. Despite these barriers peers demonstrated a strong intrinsic motivation rooted in altruism for their work. Many peers reported living paycheck to paycheck with some relying on secondary income sources to remain in the role. The combination of low pay, high emotional labor, and limited upward mobility raises ethical concerns about the exploitation of peer work in broader health recovery settings. This paper draws on peer experiences to highlight the need for structural reform including improved compensation, upward mobility, career pathways, and professional development to help sustain the peer workforce. Legitimizing and recognizing experiential expertise as comparable to professional experience is essential in securing the long term vitality of the peer workforce. Not applicable.

items.title: A systematic review of ergonomic interventions for reducing work-related musculoskeletal disorders among informal workers
items.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) impose a disproportionate burden on informal sector workers who lack occupational health protection. To identify and characterize ergonomic interventions applied to informal sector workers, to analyze their effectiveness in reducing WMSD outcomes by anatomical region, to evaluate the methodological quality of available evidence, and to provide evidence-based recommendations for ergonomic programs in resource-limited settings. A systematic search was conducted on 5 May 2026 across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and EBSCO using a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, and Study (PICOS) framework following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Six studies met all inclusion criteria from 29 unique articles. Due to substantial heterogeneity in study design, intervention characteristics, outcome measures, and incomplete statistical reporting, a narrative synthesis approach was adopted following Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines. All six included studies involving informal agricultural and plantation workers in Thailand ( n = 3), Malaysia ( n = 1), Iran ( n = 1), and Colombia ( n = 1) reported statistically significant improvements in at least one work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) outcome. Multicomponent interventions combining ergonomic training with workstation modification demonstrated the most favorable outcomes. Low back pain was the most frequently improved region (6/6 studies). Quality of evidence was Moderate according to the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) framework in five studies and Strong in one. Ergonomic interventions were associated with reductions in WMSDs outcomes among the studied informal worker populations, although the evidence is limited by study heterogeneity. Participatory ergonomics and multicomponent interventions showed the most favorable findings. The evidence supports implementation of context-sensitive ergonomic programs within primary healthcare and community health infrastructure in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

items.title: A Tale of Two Error Categories: Exploring Concealed Trade-Offs in the Errors of Automated Judges in Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantifiers
items.abstract: The wide adoption of LLMs across broad NLG applications heightens the importance of providing users with the means to avert errors and hallucinations. Uncertainty quantification is poised to fill that gap; with low uncertainty (high confidence), as a proxy for correctness, allowing users to be selective (e.g., reject low-confidence, likely incorrect responses). Correlation between confidence and correctness then serves as a useful criterion for evaluation of uncertainty quantifiers (UQs). But in NLG, where diverse responses can be adequate to a prompt, obtaining reliable correctness judgements is not simple, especially without human intervention. Errors in automated judgement are hardly avoidable and known to diminish the reliability of evaluation protocols (Santilli et al., 2025; Ielanskyi et al., 2025). In a meta-analysis of published work, we show that automated judgement is the present norm. Besides, automated judgements are rarely validated against human ones, and the validation of the UQ evaluation they automate is even rarer. With experiments in question answering, using 4 LLMs, human and automated judgements and 7 popular UQs, we find that i) a judge's performance can only coarsely predict the observed impact of its errors on the reliability of UQ evaluation, and that ii) judgement errors tend to misrepresent informative UQs most. We link these observations to patterns of correlation between confidence and categories of judgement error.

items.title: Achievement emotions in AI-assisted learning, academic self-efficacy, and learning engagement and AI dependence among university students in statistics-related programs: a moderated mediation study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools have become part of everyday coursework for university students, yet the emotional and motivational conditions under which these tools support or undermine learning remain poorly understood. Drawing on the control-value theory of achievement emotions, this study examined whether academic self-efficacy mediates the links of positive achievement emotions in AI-assisted learning with learning engagement and AI dependence, and whether AI literacy moderates the first stage of these pathways. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 700 undergraduate students (386 female; M_age = 19.81 years, SD = 1.27) majoring in applied statistics and related programs at three universities in Shijiazhuang, China. Participants completed measures of positive and negative achievement emotions, academic self-efficacy, learning engagement, AI dependence, and AI literacy. Confirmatory factor analysis preceded a first-stage moderated mediation analysis with bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals (5,000 resamples), controlling for negative emotions, gender, and year of study. Results The six-factor measurement model fitted the data well, χ 2 (50) = 55.62, p = 0.271, CFI = 0.998, RMSEA = 0.013, SRMR = 0.017. Positive achievement emotions predicted higher self-efficacy ( β = 0.374), which in turn predicted stronger engagement ( β = 0.395) and lower AI dependence ( β = −0.176), all p < 0.001, with AI literacy entered in every equation. AI literacy moderated the emotion-efficacy association ( β = 0.152, p < 0.001): the conditional indirect association with engagement rose from 0.088 to 0.208 across ±1 SD of AI literacy, and that with AI dependence fell from −0.039 to −0.093. The direct association with AI dependence was positive ( β = 0.447, p < 0.001), and the conditional total association remained positive (0.355 to 0.408). Both indexes of moderated mediation were significant. Conclusion Positive emotional experiences in AI-assisted coursework show beneficial and costly associations simultaneously, and self-efficacy statistically accounts for opposing parts of each. The total association with dependence remained positive at all literacy levels, so the results describe inconsistent mediation rather than protection. AI literacy marks where the emotion-engagement pathway is strongest.

items.title: Activating Social Responses in Human–AI Interaction: The Effects of Reciprocal Self-Disclosure and Social Role Framing
items.abstract: As chatbots become increasingly embedded in everyday communication, understanding when they elicit social responses is important. We conducted an experiment in which 169 participants interacted with LLM-based chatbots in a 2 (reciprocal self-disclosure: yes vs. no) × 3 (social role: mentor, companion, or assistant) between-subjects design. Self-esteem was measured before the interaction as an individual-difference factor. Factorial analyses showed that reciprocal self-disclosure increased users’ disclosure but did not significantly increase trust or perceived support; enjoyment was lower in the reciprocal-disclosure condition. Social role interacted with self-esteem in predicting self-disclosure quality, with favorable responses to the mentor role among participants with higher self-esteem. These findings suggest that chatbot social cues elicit different behavioral and evaluative responses and that role framing should account for user characteristics. The study offers a conditional account of social responding in human–AI interaction and implications for chatbot design in relational contexts.

items.title: Activation-Aware Weight Tensorization: A Calibration-Time Preconditioner for Tensor-Network LLM Compression
items.abstract: Post-training tensor-network compression replaces Transformer linear layers with Tensor Train (TT) or Tree Tensor Network (TTN) operators, but standard decompositions minimize weight-space Frobenius error rather than functional error under the layer's activation distribution. We propose Activation-aware Weight Tensorization (AWT), a training-free calibration wrapper that preconditions each weight matrix with a diagonal activation-derived scale before an unchanged TT/TTN solver and deploys the result with only an input-side elementwise rescaling. Across Llama 3.1 8B, Ministral 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, AWT consistently improves vanilla TT/TTN tensorization at 2-6 times compression: under single-operator replacement, AWT closes 12-35% of the WikiText perplexity gap to the dense baseline across the three model families and 2-6 times compression settings; while under multi-operator Llama suffix replacement it closes 27-60% across attention-group and all-seven-matrix settings. The gains also transfer to downstream HellaSwag and ARC-Challenge evaluations. We further show that diagonal preconditioning is a robustness-modularity tradeoff rather than a diagonal-covariance assumption: a dense full-covariance oracle wins its own weighted objective in 80/81 cases, yet diagonal AWT gives better held-out functional fidelity in 53/81 cases. Together, these results position AWT as a principled, modular preconditioner for improving functional fidelity in fixed TT/TTN compression pipelines without modifying the decomposition solver.

items.title: AdaT$^2$: Adaptive Test Transformations for Black-Box Boundary Testing of Conversational Agents
items.abstract: Conversational agents based on large language models (LLMs) must comply with policies. Each condition in a policy draws a boundary between user requests, and the agent must behave differently on its two sides. We present AdaT$^2$, which extracts statements from the agent's replies in exploratory conversations with an LLM acting as the user, and uses the statements to guide boundary test generation. Each statement describes one condition and the behavior expected when the condition holds. Besides plain tests guided by single statements, AdaT$^2$ writes transformed tests guided by pairs of a statement and a test transformation instruction, such as "omit one required input". The instruction of a pair can move a test to the other side of the statement's boundary or to another boundary. The statements and instructions form far more pairs than a run can try, and many pairs are not applicable. Adaptive pair selection therefore chooses the statement of each pair by novelty and the instruction with the bandit algorithm Bayes-UCB, which learns from whether earlier pairs yielded a test and whether the agent passed it according to an LLM judge. Our benchmark counts the two sides of each boundary separately and distinguishes boundaries explicitly defined by the agent's prompt, tool code, or knowledge base from boundaries that the agent's LLM infers from domain knowledge. On four domains of $τ^3$-bench, 62.7% to 83.3% of AdaT$^2$'s tests are valid boundary tests whose expected behavior is explicitly defined, higher in every domain than AgentEval's (47.7% to 68.1%). Transformed tests add 13 to 46 explicitly defined boundaries that plain tests miss. As regression tests, AdaT$^2$'s test suites detect all eight seeded policy faults in the airline domain and four of eight in the retail domain, and AgentEval's test suites, with fewer than a third as many tests, detect five and two, respectively.

items.title: AeroEval: Staged Program and Execution Validation for AI-Generated Drone Missions
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate drone programs from natural-language mission descriptions, but syntactically valid programs may still violate user intent, environmental constraints, and mission-level behavior. This problem is pronounced in cyber-physical applications, where correctness depends on the interaction among generated code, mobile sensing, environmental geometry, event-driven analytics, and physical execution. Existing drone code-generation systems primarily use prompt guardrails or simulator outcomes and provide limited failure localization. We present AeroEval, an agent-assisted middleware for staged validation of AI-generated drone missions. AeroEval combines deterministic program analysis with context-grounded LLM agents. It first validates program syntax, platform API usage, and mission intent, and then evaluates the realized behavior using execution trajectories, mission requirements, and environmental context. Each stage returns structured failure information for iterative regeneration. In our evaluation using 20 navigation tasks and five analytical mission types over AirSim and Gazebo simulators, AeroEval improves navigation success from 55% to 95%. In a stagewise ablation study, our Code and Trajectory Validators by themselves achieve mean run-level success rates of 44% and 56%, respectively, while the full AeroEval pipeline achieves 88%; the stages detect complementary failures in program structure, API usage, mission intent, obstacle avoidance, altitude, coverage, and event-driven transitions and the guided regeneration corrects for them. Across the main analytics missions, AeroEval increases aggregate run-level success from 34% for one-shot AeroGen to 88% within the regeneration budget. These results demonstrate the benefit of combining program-level and execution-grounded agentic validation for AI-generated drone applications in the evaluated environment.

items.title: Agentic AI Disaster Management
items.abstract: This project proposes an Agentic AI-based disaster management framework for real-time decision-making during floods and landslides. It integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), Multi-Agent RAG, Digital Twins, GIS, IoT, CCTV, UAVs, and satellite data to provide accurate situational awareness. Specialized AI agents analyze real-time information to identify risks, affected areas, and resource requirements. The Agentic RAG system retrieves relevant historical data, emergency procedures, maps, and disaster knowledge to support decision-making. The framework generates adaptive, evidence-based response strategies for rescue prioritization, resource allocation, evacuation, and emergency coordination.

items.title: AgentTracer: Tracing Indirect Prompt Injection Attack through Fine-Grained Intention-Execution Alignment
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents interact with external resources to complete complex user tasks, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where malicious instructions redirect agents toward attacker-intended tasks. Since IPI is difficult to defend against in real-world environments, post-incident tracing is essential for locating the injection source and reconstructing the attack chain. However, existing tracing methods primarily capture explicit control-flow and data-flow dependencies, overlooking the implicit relationships among tool calls driven by the malicious instruction. These tool calls may lack explicit dependencies and be interleaved with legitimate operations, making complete attack-chain reconstruction difficult. In this paper, we present AgentTracer, an intent-aware tracing framework that treats IPI as task intent drift. AgentTracer recovers implicit decision dependencies among tool calls to construct an Intent-Driven Execution Graph that connects dispersed tool calls by task intent. It combines the user request with an operation knowledge base to construct a user intent authorization space and identify intent-drift tool calls. Starting from an anomalous tool call under audit, AgentTracer performs target-based pruning and backward tracing to reconstruct the attack chain and locate the injection source and injection point. To evaluate AgentTracer in the presence of noise from normal tasks, we combine execution logs constructed from successful IPI attacks in AgentDyn and InjecAgent with normal execution logs containing 1,800 user requests and 9,000 background tool calls without IPI. In end-to-end experiments, AgentTracer achieves 94.17 percent injection-point accuracy and 93.56 percent path precision. Comparative experiments show that AgentTracer improves injection-point accuracy over existing methods by 18 to 54 percent.

items.title: Agreement Is Not a Criterion: What Matching Human Labels Certifies About an LLM Judge, Why a Shared Shortcut Passes the Test, and Why Every External Criterion Found So Far Validates a Use Rather Than a Judge
items.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. An automatic judge is usually accepted on one piece of evidence: it agrees with human preference labels about as often as humans agree with each other. That number is then read as permission to use the judge for ranking models, filtering data, selecting samples and supplying reward. This paper separates three claims the ritual runs together - that the judge can stand in for the labelers on a given item population, that it tracks the quality construct the labels were meant to measure, and that decisions made with it turn out well in a stated use - and argues that agreement evidence bears directly only on the first. A stylised two-loading model makes the reason exact: agreement with a single reference identifies one linear combination of a judge's sensitivity to the construct and to the surface features the labelers also respond to, so a judge that shares the labelers' shortcuts can match a judge that tracks quality. The published record is then read through that separation. Human labels carry documented surface sensitivities that judges reproduce; judges carry failures of their own that natural validation sets never exercise; and agreement is concentrated on the easy, wide-gap items where decisions matter least. In the corners where an external criterion exists - verified correctness, downstream policy outcomes, randomised business outcomes and verifiable task success - the criterion has repeatedly exposed failures that agreement did not show, and where it confirms an offline score the confirmation does not transfer across uses: a benchmark score that predicts best-of-N selection well gives only a rough signal for PPO. Validity, on this evidence, is a property of a judge in a use. The paper consolidates these published results, states a use-indexed validation procedure as an algorithm, and proposes the tests that would settle what remains open.

items.title: AI Anthropology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from specialized technical domains to today’s pervasive sociotechnical phenomenon, creating a transformative force that is reshaping the lived experience while challenging anthropology to maintain its relevance and adapt. This chapter introduces AI Anthropology as an emerging subfield that addresses this challenge through three dimensions: examining AI as a cultural artifact, leveraging AI-driven computational methods for research, and embedding anthropological insights into AI design. Through a review of anthropological literature on AI and a case study of entrepreneurial responses to generative AI, this chapter illustrates how anthropologists can actively shape technological trajectories rather than merely critique them. Further, it argues that as technological change and academic precarity intersect, AI Anthropology offers a practical framework for maintaining relevance, fostering new professional pathways, and guiding AI development in ways that respect human diversity and dignity.

items.title: AI as Market Infrastructure: How Misinformation and Automation Inequality Shape Democratic Performance and Economic Wellbeing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the market-organizing infrastructures that coordinate exchange, reshaping consumer information environments and the allocation of economic value. Drawing on marketing systems theory and consumer emancipation scholarship, we theorize perceived misinformation threat and perceived automation inequality as system-level diagnostics that erode perceived democratic performance and, through it, consumers’ perceived economic wellbeing. We further theorize national AI interpretive climates as contextual amplifiers that condition how threat cues translate into institutional skepticism or optimism. A multilevel analysis across 22 nations supports the institutional-confidence pathway and the amplifying role of collective AI beliefs. By repositioning AI from firm-level tool to structural infrastructure, the study clarifies how AI-driven market externalities become consequential for consumer welfare, advancing macromarketing theory on emancipation, marketing governance, consumer agency, and public policy in AI-mediated markets.

items.title: AI in supply chain risk assessment: a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Supply chain risk assessment (SCRA) is pivotal for ensuring resilience in increasingly complex global supply networks. While existing reviews have explored traditional methodologies, they often neglect emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications and mostly lack combined systematic and bibliometric analyses. This study addresses these gaps by integrating a systematic literature review with bibliometric analysis, examining 1,903 articles (2015-2025), with 54 studies selected through PRISMA guidelines. Our findings reveal that ML models, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and hybrid approaches, significantly improve risk prediction accuracy and adaptability in post-pandemic contexts. The bibliometric analysis identifies key trends, influential authors, and institutional contributions, highlighting China and the United States as leading research hubs. Practical insights emphasize the integration of explainable AI (XAI) for transparent decision-making, real-time data utilization, and blockchain for traceability. The study underscores the necessity of dynamic strategies, interdisciplinary collaboration, and continuous model evaluation to address challenges such as data quality and interpretability. By synthesizing AI-driven methodologies with resilience frameworks, this review provides actionable guidance for optimizing supply chain risk management, fostering adaptability, and informing future research in evolving risk landscapes.

items.title: AI readiness and digital pedagogical competence as enablers of innovations in environmental management within higher education institutions: evidence from Vietnam
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and digital pedagogical competence (DPC) are associated with lecturers’ perceptions of digital environmental governance innovation (DEGI) and perceived environmental performance in higher education institutions (HEIs). Moving beyond isolated green technologies, the study adopts a governance-oriented perspective to explain how individual digital capabilities among academic staff are linked to perceived sustainability-related outcomes through digitally enabled environmental governance innovation. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 1,525 academic staff working in Vietnamese HEIs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was used to test the proposed capability–governance–perception framework and to examine both direct and indirect relationships among the constructs. Findings The findings indicate that AI readiness (artificial intelligence readiness) is positively associated with DPC and lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI. DPC is also positively associated with governance innovation. Most importantly, lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI are strongly associated with perceived environmental performance and indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AIR and perceived environmental outcomes within the specified model. Research limitations/implications This study is based on cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from a single national context, which limits causal inference and statistical generalisability. The findings should therefore be interpreted as perception-based associations rather than evidence of objectively measured institutional environmental improvement. Future research could adopt longitudinal, comparative, multi-source or objective-indicator designs. Practical implications The findings suggest that HEIs should move beyond technology adoption alone and invest in human digital capabilities, sustainability dashboards, environmental data reporting systems and governance structures. Strengthening AIR and DPC among academic staff may support digitally mediated governance innovations for environmental management. Social implications By highlighting governance innovation as a perception-based pathway linking digital capabilities to perceived environmental performance, this study offers insights for HEIs seeking to strengthen their sustainability responsibilities. Digitally enabled environmental governance may support broader sustainability transitions, provided it is embedded within accountable institutional practices. Originality/value This study offers empirical evidence linking individual digital capabilities to perceived environmental management outcomes in higher education through governance innovation. It extends sustainability and digital transformation research by positioning AIR and DPC as enablers of perceived digitally driven environmental governance, particularly within a Global South context.

items.title: AI tools drive innovation in sports firms through employee experiences moderated by perceived digital transformation climate
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigates how artificial intelligence tools improve perceived innovation capability within sports firms, focusing on the parallel mediating roles of workplace enjoyment and supportive climate, organizational identification, and AI-enhanced work engagement, and the moderating role of perceived digital transformation climate. Drawing on Social Identity Theory and the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, we argue that AI functions as a vital organizational resource, triggering three parallel pathways toward innovation: affective, identity-based, and motivational. We collected survey data from 611 employees of Chinese sports enterprises and analyzed the data using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Results reveal that AI significantly enhances perceived innovation capability directly and indirectly through workplace enjoyment and supportive climate, organizational identification, and AI-enhanced work engagement, among which organizational identification showed the largest indirect point estimate, though pairwise contrasts were not statistically significant. In addition, perceived digital transformation climate positively moderates the direct association between artificial intelligence tools and perceived innovation capability. These findings provide an integrated framework for unpacking AI-enabled innovation in sports organizations, emphasizing the importance of employees’ workplace experience and strategic perceived digital transformation climate. Theoretical contributions and practical managerial implications for sports-sector digital innovation are discussed.

items.title: AI-Assisted Submissions in Online Research Are Rare and Highly Concentrated but Routinely Approved
items.abstract: Online research platforms underpin much of what science claims about people, on the assumption that a human produced each response. Generative AI threatens that assumption by letting participants delegate responses to a chatbot, yet how often they do so remains unclear because prior estimates rely on self-report or automated detection rather than direct observation. We surveyed 2,500 workers on a high quality online research platform and directly observed AI assistance by linking donated ChatGPT histories to platform submission records of weekly ChatGPT users, covering 712,930 submissions across more than 127,000 studies. Although one in eight surveyed workers reported ever using AI on a study and 68% of observed workers had done so, assistance appeared in only 1% of submissions, with no detectable increase over more than 3 years. Assistance was often temporally localized within tasks and highly concentrated among workers, with 5% accounting for 64% of assisted submissions. Where assistance occurred, workers were virtually always paid, even when study instructions prohibited AI use, with overall approval rates similar to those for unassisted submissions. Half of assisted submissions involved bounded responses, outside the scope of the platform's LLM detector for open-ended responses. Taken together, our results do not support the view that AI assistance currently poses an existential threat to online research, but reveal limited payment consequences for prohibited use and gaps in platform safeguards, leaving platforms poorly prepared should that threat materialize.

items.title: AI-Augmented Peer Review by Orthogonal Constraint: A Retrospective Case Study of Mathematical, Concordance, Chemical, and Meta-Review
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence in scientific writing and mathematical formalization creates a corresponding need for review methods capable of validating rapidly generated, multidisciplinary technical work. We present and retrospectively evaluate an AI-augmented peer-review architecture in which distinct review stages are assigned orthogonal objectives: mathematical correctness, concordance with an established formal framework, chemical admissibility of molecular claims, targeted verification of revisions, and final meta-review. The method is examined through the development of The Chrysene Formalism Revisited: A Twelve-Axiom Foundation for Molecular Characterization, Tensorial Noncommutative Geometry, and Operator Response, a manuscript whose mathematical development is externally constrained by a molecular reference structure. The complete review trajectory was reconstructed as a coded revision ledger. Sixty-four review/process actions were identified, of which 63 were manuscript-directed. Twenty-two revisions (34.9%) were classified as major, 20 (31.7%) as structural, and 59 (93.7%) were fully adopted. Forty-eight actions (76.2%) were explicitly verified in a subsequent review cycle, increasing to 55 (87.3%) when indirect later verification was included. The review disciplines generated markedly different correction profiles. Mathematics produced 35 of the 63 manuscript-directed actions and accounted for all coded proof/analytic repairs and theorem-strength corrections. Concordance generated nine actions, all of which were major and structural, including every action classified as structural restoration. Chemistry generated eight actions concentrated primarily in molecular qualification and nomenclature. The pivotal event was the failure of a mathematically improved manuscript to pass concordance review, requiring substantial reconstruction before renewed chemistry and mathematics review. The case therefore suggests that the value of AI augmentation may lie not simply in increasing review volume, but in separating validation objectives, preserving reviewer disagreement as diagnostic information, distinguishing criticism from revision and verification, and maintaining an auditable record of manuscript development. Because this is a single retrospective case study without a conventional peer-review control group, the results do not establish the superiority of AI-augmented review. They instead provide a reproducible framework for prospective evaluation across future manuscripts.

items.title: AI-INDUCED ACADEMIC DEVIANCE: A CRIMINOLOGICAL STUDY ON CHANGES IN STUDENTS’ LIFE ACTIVITIES AND CONDUCT
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) affects academic deviance among criminology students at the University of the Visayas. Using a quantitative research design, it gathered data from 278 randomly selected respondents to assess how AI tools affect students’ study habits, academic integrity, and ethical decision-making. The results show that AI can make learning more efficient and effective, but it also brings risks such as academic dishonesty, overreliance on technology, and reduced independent thinking, problem-solving, and creativity. ChatGPT is the AI tool respondents use most often, showing that conversational AI is becoming more popular in academic settings. The study also finds that students with some experience using AI understand its benefits and challenges, but they do not have advanced skills or a strong understanding of ethics. Gender and year level play important roles in how students use AI. Even though institutions try to encourage ethical use of AI, there is still a gap between what policies say and what actually happens. The study suggests adding AI literacy, ethical guidelines, and monitoring systems to academic programs. This approach supports responsible AI use, protects academic integrity, and helps future criminology professionals think independently. These findings are meant to guide educational strategies and policies as digital learning becomes more common.

items.abstract: The cost of study abroad has been a barrier to access for a greater number of students. As a high-impact program, alternative access to study abroad should be pressing. Literature considers study abroad and artificial intelligence in isolation of each other; indicating a deeper widening research gap challenging artificial intelligence as not adequately fitted for alternate resource. Review methodology were limited to high-quality academic research databases. The findings revealed that AI has the capacity to expand access to study abroad through state agency support for institutions, and personalized learning. Access can be enhanced when institutions reverse from operating AI as an isolation, but as exploration of study abroad. Advancing AI supported study abroad programs requires greater investment in technological infrastructure and resources.

items.title: Alice: A Large-Scale German Benchmark for Rubric-Based Multi-Dimensional Automatic Short Answer Scoring
items.abstract: Automatic Short Answer Scoring (ASAS) is central to NLP for Education. However, openly available benchmarks remain scarce, and existing datasets largely address how well students answer a question directly rather than how well they master underlying concepts (knowledge elements) such as thermal energy or epistemic activities (skills) such as reasoning or claim. To address this gap, we introduce Alice, a large-scale, rubric-based German ASAS dataset that is pedagogically aligned and comprises three subtasks: (i) learning performance (Alice-LP), (ii) knowledge elements (Alice-KE), and (iii) skills (Alice-SK). We further formulate rubric-based ASAS as a rubric-retrieval task and benchmark the dataset with a range of language models, from encoder-only models to lightweight LLMs. We also benchmark the dataset with zero-shot prompting via LLMs and a standard classification baseline. The experiments show that LLMs, in particular, struggle to score knowledge elements and skills in the zero-shot setting. They also indicate that rubric text is often useful, especially for Alice-KE and Alice-SK, while on Alice-LP gains over sample-solution-focused inputs are more modest and vary by model and input format.

items.title: Ambedkar Beyond April 14: Equality in the Age of AI and Gen Z India
items.abstract: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is widely commemorated through symbolic rituals, yet his radical paradigm of social justice remains underutilised as a critical framework for contemporary structural challenges. In 2026 India, rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), automated decision-making, and digital public infrastructure (DPI) have transformed socio-political and economic relations. However, stark disparities in digital infrastructure, algorithmic transparency, and literacy have codified new, technocratic layers of inequality that deeply impact India's Gen Z demographic. This study examines technological inequality through a structural reinterpretation of Ambedkar’s philosophy of social justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity. Utilising an analytical evaluation of institutional datasets spanning 2018-2025, we map rural-urban divides, pedagogical gaps, economic asymmetries in enterprise and agriculture, and localised algorithmic biases. The article argues that inclusive, democratised technological governance is not merely a policy preference but a constitutional imperative required to preserve human dignity in an increasingly automated state. Keywords: Ambedkar; Artificial Intelligence; Digital Equality; Gen Z; Social Justice; India

items.title: Ambivalent acceptance of active exoskeletons in long-term care: between perceived task-specific support and practical constraints
items.abstract: Background Lower back pain (LBP) is prevalent among nursing staff in long-term care facilities. This condition has been linked to repetitive resident handling, sustained non-neutral postures, and cumulative physical workloads. Despite growing interest in exoskeletons as ergonomic and digital assistive technologies (DAT), evidence regarding the implementation of active exoskeletons in real-world nursing practice remains limited. Objective The objective of this exploratory mixed-methods feasibility study was to evaluate the implementation of the HAL® Lumbar Type active exoskeleton in long-term care settings. Specifically, this study explored feasibility, usability, nurses’ acceptance, and descriptive pain-related outcomes under real-world conditions. Methods A non-randomized exploratory mixed-methods feasibility study was conducted in three long-term residential care facilities in Germany. The HAL® Lumbar Type was introduced for use in routine nursing practice during a 90-day intervention period. Objective utilization and adherence data were not systematically recorded. Quantitative outcomes ( n = 15) included subjective LBP, functional impairment, and health-related quality of life measured using the visual analog scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and 8-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-8), respectively. A qualitative semi-structured interview study ( n = 9) explored participants’ experiences of usability, workflow integration, and acceptance. Qualitative data were analyzed using systematic text condensation. Results The findings suggested a pattern of ambivalent acceptance. Caregivers reported situational support during forward-leaning and transfer-related activities, particularly through perceived postural stabilization. The aggregated unpaired VAS data showed no descriptive group-level reduction in subjective pain, and individual pain trajectories could not be assessed. Some participants had lower ODI scores at follow-up, whereas the SF-8 trajectories were heterogeneous and partially indicated a lower health-related quality of life. Participants described spatial limitations, device weight, thermal discomfort, restricted mobility, and the time required for donning and adjustment as barriers to routine use. Participants reported using the exoskeleton selectively for specific high-load tasks rather than continuously throughout shifts. Conclusion The active lumbar exoskeleton was perceived to provide task-specific ergonomic or postural support during selected physical care activities. However, participants’ accounts suggested that the perceived practical viability of the device and their willingness to use it may be associated with workflow compatibility, ease of use, perceived fit, and organizational conditions. Long-term adoption beyond the intervention period was not assessed. Future advancements in exoskeleton technology should prioritize lightweight designs, customized fits, and seamless integration strategies into dynamic nursing workflows. Larger longitudinal studies with appropriate comparison groups and objective biomechanical measures are needed to determine the clinical effectiveness and further examine implementation conditions in nursing practice.

items.title: An Analysis of the Safe System
items.abstract: The purpose of this chapter is to analyse the Safe System in road safety as it is related to the topic addressed in this handbook: how to apply an understanding of human factors to the design and management of roads. Road safety is a complex system; by looking at the elements of the Safe System, it is concluded that it oversimplifies both the scope of road safety and the tasks required to significantly reduce road trauma. An assessment of the Safe System against the previous “traditional” approach concludes that an understanding of cognitive human factors (as they relate to road design and traffic management) plays no part in the Safe System, which focuses primarily (though not exclusively) on reducing the consequences of crashes, nor is seeking to address the causes of crashes a part of it. The Safe System regards human error as inevitable, which leaves no scope for road designs and traffic management techniques to be adjusted to avoid errors that lead to crashes. As many practitioners still seek to prevent crashes from happening, it is concluded that they are applying a hybrid of the traditional approach and the Safe System.
